Chapter Six. Advanced Tidying—Navigating Komono and Sentimental Items with Care.
Now that you’ve worked through the basic categories, it’s time to turn your attention to the trickier stuff—the things that don’t fit neatly into a single box. We’re talking about komono, those miscellaneous odds and ends scattered all over the place, and of course, the sentimental treasures that tug at your heart.
Let’s start with komono. You know, the kitchen gadgets, hobby supplies, tangled cords, tools, beauty products—basically, everything from your favorite pen to that random charger you found in a drawer last week. These items sneak into every corner, quietly piling up until you barely notice how many you have.
Here’s the trick: just like before, gather every similar item from every part of your home, and group them by type—maybe all your electronics in one pile, your stationery in another, and so on. It’s amazing what you’ll find when you see it all together! Suddenly, those duplicates jump out, and you get a much clearer sense of what you actually use.
When you’re sorting through komono, the joy principle still matters, but practicality steps up, too. Maybe your spatula doesn’t exactly make your heart sing, but think about how handy it is every morning when you make breakfast. The things you keep should genuinely serve you and make your daily life run smoother. If something’s just taking up space or adding clutter, it might be time to let it go.
Now, let’s talk about sentimental items—photos, letters, souvenirs, and keepsakes. These are saved for last for a reason. Each piece holds a memory or a story, and picking them up might stir up all kinds of feelings, from laughter to tears.
It’s so important to approach this part gently. Maybe set aside some quiet time, create a cozy space, and give yourself room to reflect and remember. Here are a few ways to make it easier:
Try holding each memento and let yourself recall the moment it represents. What do you feel? Does this item still support the person you are today—or is it connected to someone you used to be?
You might want to keep just a few special things that really capture the essence of those memories. And if it’s time to say goodbye to something, thank it for what it’s given you. Trust that the memory itself will stay, even if the object doesn’t.
By moving through komono and sentimental items with care, you’re not just tidying up—you’re honoring your past while making thoughtful choices for your future. Little by little, your home becomes a reflection of what matters most to you—both the memories you cherish and the life you want to live right now.
